\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Stability curve]
\lean{FABL.stabilityCurve}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p053-b005,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p056-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p124-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p214-b006,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p214-b007
}
\label{FABL.stabilityCurve}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.fourierCoeff}
For a real-valued function $f$ on the $n$-dimensional Boolean cube, its stability curve
at $\rho\in\mathbb{R}$ is $\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\rho^{|S|}\widehat f(S)^2$, where
$\widehat f(S)$ is the Fourier coefficient indexed by $S$.
\end{definition}

\difficulty{1}
Let $f$ be a real-valued function on the $n$-dimensional sign cube and let
$\rho\in[-1,1]$. Write $\widehat f(S)$ for its Fourier coefficient at a coordinate set
$S$. The stability curve $\sum_S \rho^{|S|}\widehat f(S)^2$ equals the expected product
$f(X)f(Y)$ when $X$ is uniform on the sign cube and, independently in each coordinate,
$Y_i$ equals $X_i$ with probability $(1+\rho)/2$ and $-X_i$ otherwise.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Stability derivative at zero]
\lean{FABL.deriv_stabilityCurve_zero}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p124-b004,

\difficulty{4}
For any real-valued function $f$ on the $n$-dimensional sign cube, let $\widehat f(S)$
denote its uniform Fourier coefficients and define
$S_f(\rho)=\sum_{A\subseteq[n]}\rho^{|A|}\widehat f(A)^2$. Then
$S_f'(0)=\sum_{i=1}^n\widehat f(\{i\})^2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Noise stability under sign reversal]
\lean{FABL.noiseStability_neg}
\label{FABL.noiseStability_neg}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.monomial, FABL.noiseStability, FABL.noiseStability_eq_sum_rho_pow_mul_sq_fourierCoeff}
\difficulty{4}
For every correlation parameter $\rho\in[-1,1]$ and every real-valued function $f$ on
the Boolean cube, the noise stability of $-f$ equals that of $f$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $0<\rho<1$, and let $f$ be a function from the
$n$-dimensional sign cube to $\{\pm1\}$. If the mean of the real-valued function $f$ is
zero, then the noise stability of $f$ at correlation $\rho$ is at most $\rho$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Noise stability and signed dictators]

\difficulty{6}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $0<\rho<1$, and let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}$ be
balanced, meaning that its mean under the uniform measure on the cube is zero. Form a
correlated pair $(X,Y)$ by choosing $X$ uniformly and, independently in each coordinate,
keeping its sign with probability $(1+\rho)/2$ and flipping it otherwise. Then
$\mathbb{E}[f(X)f(Y)]=\rho$ if and only if there is a coordinate $i$ such that
$f(x)=x_i$ for every $x$, or $f(x)=-x_i$ for every $x$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{3}
For any real-valued function $f$ on the $n$-dimensional sign cube, let $\widehat f(S)$
denote its uniform Fourier coefficients and define the stability curve
$S_f(\rho)=\sum_{A\subseteq[n]}\rho^{|A|}\widehat f(A)^2$. Define
$I(f)=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb{E}[((f(x^{i,+})-f(x^{i,-}))/2)^2]$, where $x^{i,+}$ and
$x^{i,-}$ are obtained by setting coordinate $i$ to $+1$ and $-1$, respectively. Then
$S_f'(1)=I(f)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Stable influence]
\lean{FABL.stableInfluence}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p057-b001,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p145-b008,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p215-b005,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p264-b003
}
\label{FABL.stableInfluence}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.fourierCoeff}
For $\rho\in\mathbb{R}$, a real-valued function $f$ on the $n$-dimensional Boolean cube,
and a coordinate $i\in[n]$, its stable influence at $i$ is $\sum_{S\subseteq[n]: i\in
S}\rho^{|S|-1}\widehat f(S)^2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Equivalence of subsets containing and avoiding a coordinate]
\lean{FABL.eraseContainingEquiv}
\label{FABL.eraseContainingEquiv}
\leanok
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $i\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$. The finite subsets of
$\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ containing $i$ are in bijection with those avoiding $i$, by deleting
$i$ in one direction and adjoining it in the other.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Total stable influence]
\lean{FABL.totalStableInfluence}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p057-b001,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p215-b005,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p268-b001
}
\label{FABL.totalStableInfluence}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.stableInfluence}
For $\rho\in\mathbb{R}$ and a real-valued function $f$ on the $n$-dimensional Boolean
cube, its total stable influence is the sum of its stable influences over all
coordinates $i\in[n]$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Nonnegativity of stable influence]
\lean{FABL.stableInfluence_nonneg}
\label{FABL.stableInfluence_nonneg}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.stableInfluence}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $f:\{−1,1\}^n\to\mathbb R$, and let $i$ be a
coordinate. For every $\rho\in[0,1]$, the stable influence of $f$ at parameter $\rho$
and coordinate $i$ is nonnegative; here stable influence is the sum, over coordinate
subsets containing $i$, of $\rho^{|S|-1}$ times the square of the uniform Fourier
coefficient of $f$ on $S$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Nonnegativity of total stable influence]
\lean{FABL.totalStableInfluence_nonneg}
\label{FABL.totalStableInfluence_nonneg}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.stableInfluence_nonneg, FABL.totalStableInfluence}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $f$ be a real-valued function on $\{-1,1\}^n$,
and let $0\le\rho\le 1$. The total stable influence of $f$ at parameter $\rho$ is
nonnegative.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{5}

\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $f$ be a real-valued function on $\{-1,1\}^n$
with variance at most $1$, and let $0<\delta\le 1$. Then the total stable influence of
$f$ at parameter $1-\delta$ is at most $1/\delta$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Bound on the number of large stable influences]
\lean{FABL.card_stableInfluence_ge_le}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p215-b007}
\label{FABL.card_stableInfluence_ge_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.stableInfluence, FABL.stableInfluence_nonneg, FABL.totalStableInfluence, FABL.totalStableInfluence_one_sub_le_inv, FABL.variance}
\difficulty{4}
Let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb R$ have variance at most $1$, and let
$\delta,\varepsilon\in(0,1]$. The number of coordinates whose stable influence at
parameter $1-\delta$ is at least $\varepsilon$ is at most $1/(\delta\varepsilon)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Noise sensitivity curve]
\lean{FABL.noiseSensitivityCurve}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p054-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p130-b005
}
\label{FABL.noiseSensitivityCurve}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.stabilityCurve}
For a function $f:\{-1,1	o\mathbb R$ and a real parameter $\delta$, define its noise
sensitivity curve by $\bigl(1-C_f(1-2\delta)\bigr)/2$, where $C_f$ is the stability
curve of $f$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Noise sensitivity and its curve]
\lean{FABL.noiseSensitivityCurve_eq_noiseSensitivity}
\label{FABL.noiseSensitivityCurve_eq_noiseSensitivity}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.noiseSensitivity, FABL.noiseSensitivityCurve, FABL.noiseSensitivity_eq_half_sub_half_noiseStability, FABL.stabilityCurve_eq_noiseStability}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $f$ be a function from the $n$-dimensional sign cube to
$\{ -1,1\}$, and let $0\le\delta\le1$. The noise sensitivity curve of the real-valued
version of $f$ at $\delta$ equals the noise sensitivity of $f$ at $\delta$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{3}
For any real-valued function $f$ on the $n$-dimensional sign cube, let $\widehat f(S)$
denote its uniform Fourier coefficients and define
$N_f(\delta)=\bigl(1-\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}(1-2\delta)^{|S|}\widehat f(S)^2\bigr)/2$.
Define the total influence by
$I(f)=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb{E}[((f(x^{i,+})-f(x^{i,-}))/2)^2]$, where $x^{i,+}$ and
$x^{i,-}$ are obtained by setting coordinate $i$ to $+1$ and $-1$, respectively. Then
$N_f'(0)=I(f)$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{4}
For every Boolean function $f$ on the $n$-dimensional sign cube, its noise-sensitivity
curve is monotone on $[0,1/2]$: whenever $0\le \delta_1\le\delta_2\le 1/2$, the noise
sensitivity at $\delta_1$ is at most that at $\delta_2$.
\end{theorem}
